## Simple explanation

Model serving is how an application makes a trained model available to users
or other software. It accepts inputs, runs inference, and returns outputs
through an interface such as an API or an on-device library.

## Technical explanation

A serving system packages or loads model artifacts and exposes inference
through online requests, batch jobs, or embedded execution. It manages
preprocessing, runtime dependencies, resource allocation, concurrency,
versioning, and failure handling. In LLM serving, token generation, KV-cache
memory, and batching are additional concerns.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

A model's practical value depends on whether it can be called reliably within
latency, throughput, cost, and availability requirements. Serving decisions
also affect rollout safety, hardware utilization, and how easily models can
be updated or rolled back.

## How it works

The service receives a request, validates and transforms the input, invokes
the model, and formats the result. It may batch compatible requests, scale
replicas with traffic, and emit telemetry. Online serving handles requests
interactively; batch serving processes many inputs asynchronously.

## Practical example

A recommendation API receives a user and candidate items, builds the
required feature inputs, runs a ranking model, and returns an ordered list.
The service records latency and errors without exposing sensitive data.

## Common misconceptions

- Model serving is not just loading model weights; preprocessing, dependencies, and operational behavior also matter.
- A high-throughput configuration may increase individual request latency.
- A successfully loaded model is not necessarily ready for production traffic.
